title: Certified Multimodal Robustness: Defending Vision-Language Models Against Cross-Modal Adversarial Attacks via Inconsistency Detection
background:
Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP, BLIP-2, and LLaVA have become foundational components in safety-critical pipelines including content moderation, autonomous driving, medical triage, and embodied agents. Recent work has shown that these models inherit and amplify the adversarial vulnerabilities of their unimodal predecessors: imperceptible pixel perturbations can flip zero-shot classifications [1], and adversarial suffixes appended to text prompts can jailbreak instruction-tuned VLMs into producing harmful content [2]. More troublingly, cross-modal attacks exploit the joint embedding geometry to craft image-text pairs that are individually benign but jointly malicious, evading single-modality detectors [3]. The attack surface expands further with patch attacks, typographic attacks, and adversarial ICL demonstrations that transfer across model families.

Defenses have lagged behind. Empirical methods such as adversarial fine-tuning of CLIP encoders [4] improve robustness on narrow threat models but degrade clean zero-shot accuracy and fail under adaptive attacks. Certified defenses based on randomized smoothing have been extended to multimodal settings [5], yet existing certificates either treat modalities independently, yielding loose joint bounds, or scale poorly past 224x224 inputs and short captions. Inconsistency-based detection, which flags inputs whose visual and textual semantics disagree under the model's own representations [6], shows promise but lacks formal guarantees and is brittle when the adversary controls both modalities simultaneously.

Key gaps remain: (i) there is no unified threat model that captures coordinated cross-modal perturbations under realistic semantic constraints; (ii) certified robustness radii for joint image-text inputs are orders of magnitude smaller than empirical attack budgets; (iii) inconsistency detectors have no provable false-positive or false-negative guarantees and can be bypassed by attacks optimized against the detector itself. Closing these gaps is essential before VLMs can be safely deployed in adversarial environments.
challenges: Formalizing a unified cross-modal threat model that bounds adversarial perturbations in the joint image-text semantic space rather than independent Lp balls, while remaining tight enough to admit non-vacuous certificates for production-scale VLMs (>1B parameters, 336px+ images, multi-turn dialogues).

Deriving scalable certified robustness guarantees for joint multimodal inputs that compose vision and language smoothing distributions without exponential sample complexity, and that maintain certified accuracy above 50% at perturbation budgets matching state-of-the-art empirical attacks (e.g., epsilon=8/255 plus 5-token text edits).

Designing multimodal inconsistency detectors with provable false-positive/false-negative bounds under adaptive adversaries who jointly optimize image and text perturbations against both the VLM and the detector, including detection of stealthy typographic, patch, and embedding-aligned attacks.

Preserving clean-task utility (zero-shot classification, VQA, captioning, grounding) while applying certified defenses, given that current adversarial fine-tuning incurs 10-20% absolute drops on standard benchmarks such as ImageNet zero-shot and VQAv2.

Establishing reproducible evaluation protocols and adaptive attack benchmarks for multimodal robustness, since current leaderboards rely on transfer attacks that systematically overestimate defense strength under white-box adaptive evaluation.
